If you say that empathy is the complete source of morality, then I think you run into problems. There are huge problems with empathy, being that it's usually socially determined and in unhelpful ways. Consider the rampant racism in America or anti-immigrant sentiment in Great Britain. I think they're being empathic, but not with "the other." Moreover, and this is more a Peter Singer objection, empathy is not triggered with people across the globe. So despite the fact that our money and energy could help food, clean water, and basic healthcare around the world, we let our sentiments be moved to do whatever is more partial to us.

If you say that empathy is a part of morality, almost everyone would agree. Aristotle agrees. And Kant even agrees. Even though he things Reason is the source of absolute, universal morality, he admits that empathy and virtue are important in the practical side of living morally.

I think saying "empathy" gets us to feel the warm-fuzzies. But it's an idea that's often more trouble than it's worth.
